history.heading: Pleasant Island
paragraphs: Nauru, a single raised coral island in the central Pacific, was settled by Micronesian and Polynesian peoples. British whaler John Fearn called it "Pleasant Island" in 1798. Germany annexed it in 1888.

Rich phosphate deposits, formed from ancient bird droppings, were discovered in 1900, and mining began in 1906. After the First World War, Australia, Britain and New Zealand administered Nauru jointly. Japan occupied it during the Second World War and deported many Nauruans to Chuuk.

history.heading: Independence and boom
paragraphs: Nauru became independent on 31 January 1968 and took control of phosphate mining. For a time in the 1970s and 1980s, Nauruans had one of the highest incomes per person in the world. But revenues were mismanaged, and as phosphate ran out, the country faced bankruptcy in the 2000s. Mining left about 80 percent of the island as a barren landscape of limestone pinnacles.

culture.heading: Island society
paragraphs: Nauruan and English are spoken. The population of about 12,000 is organised into 12 clans. Most people are Christian. Australian rules football is the national sport. Health problems linked to a diet of imported processed food, including very high rates of obesity and diabetes, are a major concern.

politics.heading: Parliamentary republic
paragraphs: Nauru is the world's smallest republic and the third-smallest country by area. Parliament elects the president, who is both head of state and government. It has no official capital; government offices are in Yaren. In 2024 Nauru switched diplomatic recognition from Taiwan to China. A 2024 treaty gives Australia a role in Nauru's security.

economy.heading: After phosphate
paragraphs: With phosphate largely exhausted, Nauru's economy depends on Australian aid and payments for hosting an Australian offshore immigration detention centre, fishing licences and a trust fund. It has explored deep-sea mining and selling citizenship. The currency is the Australian dollar.
